title: Who Governs Big Tech? Hannah Bloch-Wehba on AI Regulation, Police Surveillance, and Public Accountability
author: Hannah Bloch-Wehba

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not substantively assess jagged legal-AI capability, verification, or task-level work redesign. Its principal argument instead reframes the priority around private technology power, public accountability, and information governance, advocating complementary disclosure, researcher-access and regulatory-reporting mechanisms. Moore’s separate support for risk-based legal-organisation policies overlaps with the cluster’s governance point but does not establish the cluster’s broader proposition.
qs: So one of the arguments I make in the paper is that tech companies are really enmeshed in providing the informational infrastructure for government decision making.

st.an: The supplied excerpt only directs listeners to Bloch-Wehba’s work and contains no substantive claims about organisational adaptation, human control, employment, training, pricing or AI adoption. It therefore provides insufficient evidence to assess her position relative to the cluster proposition.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s governance proposition by advocating readable, risk-differentiated AI policies rather than blanket prohibitions. It adds practical emphasis on lawyers being able to explain those policies to clients, while offering advisory observations rather than measured evidence of enforcement or effectiveness.
qs: A trend we’re seeing at the moment is a shift away from policies written in 2023 and 2024, which largely stated what you couldn’t do, and toward a more informative approach that defines different risk categories and makes distinctions between routine, low-risk uses of AI and other, more substantial use cases.
One of the bigger challenges we’re seeing right now is how to express an AI use policy in such a way that any member of your legal team could explain it to a client.

kp.k: Government support helped create dependence on technology companies
kp.d: Discussing “How Tech Took Over,” Hannah Bloch-Wehba argues that deregulation alone cannot explain technology companies’ role in public governance. She traces federal support to science and innovation policies of the 1930s and ’40s, including research institutions, the National Science Foundation Act and military funding of basic research. Government became a major consumer of the innovations it supported. She qualifies this historical account as neither predictable nor linear, with changing balances between economic progress and national security.
qs: Once that ball started rolling, the government became a primary consumer of those innovations.
I think that set the stage for tech’s expansion, but not in a predictable or linear way.
The conventional narrative that the federal government has deregulated doesn’t capture what’s going on.

kp.d: Bloch-Wehba argues that technology companies supplying government’s informational infrastructure occupy a position that conventional state action doctrine and contractor analogies handle poorly. Cloud infrastructure supplied by a handful of companies illustrates the difficulty of separating public authority from private infrastructure. She identifies limited public visibility and insufficient doctrinal and scholarly attention, rather than offering a settled constitutional test.
qs: tech companies are really enmeshed in providing the informational infrastructure for government decision making.

It’s much easier to apply the traditional state action doctrine when you have a traditional government contractor relationship than when the contractors are providing the thing that makes the government run, and that is, to a significant extent, what’s happening right now.
At the same time, a lot of those infrastructural activities are hard for normal people to see and understand.

kp.k: Infrastructure lock-in constrains political accountability and competition
kp.d: Bloch-Wehba describes long-duration technology contracts and switching costs as constraints on subsequent elected administrations. Her Department of the Interior–Google cloud contract is explicitly hypothetical, not a documented procurement example. She frames this dependence as a problem accumulated over decades rather than one specific administration’s creation.
qs: This is not a Trump administration problem. This is a problem that has been occurring and building, as I argue, over decades, right?
Now imagine the entire informational infrastructure of a federal government agency is locked into one provider. It’s hard to destabilize that relationship.
Regardless of what elected officials might want to do, there are serious switching costs and serious anti-competitive effects.

kp.k: Public provision offers an alternative governance model
kp.d: Explicitly disclaiming comparative expertise, Bloch-Wehba suggests government provision of infrastructure or state control tied to public investment as alternatives to US dependence on private suppliers. She also questions treating US state action doctrine as an inevitable boundary of constitutional constraint. Her account of European audiences and changing attitudes toward US platforms is observational and qualified, not a systematic comparative study.
qs: So I’m not a comparativist, but I do think when I’ve talked about this issue in front of European audiences, they’ve been baffled.
So one model is for the government to build it themselves or to recognize that government investments give rise to a certain degree of state control.
So there’s no reason why you have to have that doctrine as the delineator of what’s subject to constitutional constraint and what’s not.

kp.k: Trade secrecy obstructs defense challenges and public validation
kp.d: Discussing privately developed tools used in criminal enforcement, Bloch-Wehba argues that vendor trade secrecy claims can prevent defendants from examining and challenging evidence used to arrest or convict them. She identifies a second, systemic harm: where tools lack meaningful pre-use testing, adversarial proceedings are a route to public knowledge about their validity, and secrecy obstructs that route too. The transcript supplies no quantified prevalence or accuracy findings.
qs: They can’t do that because the trade secrecy claim stands in their way.

It undermines their ability to challenge the evidence against them, but it also creates a bigger, more systemic problem, which is that a lot of these tools aren’t tested or validated in a meaningful way before they get used.
The process of confrontation between the defense and the prosecution is the way the public gets information about whether this tool works or not.

kp.k: Google’s data practices shaped geofence policing
kp.d: Bloch-Wehba presents geofence warrants as an example of private control over investigative capabilities and legal procedures. In her account, Google’s location-data collection and storage enabled these investigations, while its corporate policy required warrants and established the disclosure process. She says Google changed its storage practices in 2023, making the practice unavailable. Although she endorses the warrant requirement and regards the subsequent change as beneficial to privacy, her criticism concerns the absence of democratic control over these choices.
qs: Only because Google had made that choice was it possible for government to do.
This is not Google trying to apply a ruling that was already made. It’s Google saying, “This is what we want you to do.”
Then, in 2023, Google decided, “You know what? We aren’t going to do this anymore. It’s incredibly burdensome for us.” They turned off default storage of location information in the Sensorvault.

Again, I think that was a win for privacy. I don’t think it’s a win for democratic control to have individual tech companies determining, based on what’s convenient for them, whether they’re going to comply with a warrant, what legal standards should apply, and whether the government should be able to get this data.

kp.d: Responding to Greg Lambert’s comparison between corporate policy changes and individual criminal liability, Bloch-Wehba explicitly rejects criminalizing a decision to delete one’s information. Her concern is potentially uneven application of law to companies and individuals, including corporate product testing that may violate law without comparable accountability. She also criticizes reliance on lengthy terms of service as a basis for treating corporate conduct differently.
qs: I don’t think it should be a crime to decide you’re going to delete your information.
But I definitely don’t think we should have one set of rules that apply to big tech companies and a different set of rules entirely that apply to individuals.

But it is true that these companies are making decisions about, you know, how to test their products that may end up violating the law and they’re not being held to account the way that an individual might be.

kp.k: AI accountability requires complementary information mechanisms
kp.d: Bloch-Wehba describes a project examining every proposed and enacted state AI bill a couple of years before the interview, without giving a count or precise coverage dates. She interprets these measures as requiring providers to generate and disclose information to different audiences, sometimes with unclear definitions of the provider. Rather than ranking audits, impact assessments and other mechanisms, she advocates complementary public information, researcher access and regulator disclosures, grounded in an integrated conception of information law.
qs: by information law, I mean the body of legal structures that governs how knowledge is produced, validated, and disseminated.
I decided to do a project where I looked at every piece of proposed and enacted state legislation about AI.
I wrote the paper to explain that these different ways of producing information serve different purposes and should be used in complementary ways.
We need expert insight into how they’re working. That’s researcher access to the under-the-hood data a lot of the time.
I think it’s important for these companies to produce information directly to the regulators charged with overseeing their operations.

kp.k: Political and litigation pressure threatens state AI experimentation
kp.d: Bloch-Wehba maintains that states have a strong claim to regulatory capacity but describes threats of litigation, preemption and funding cuts as deterrents to experimentation. At the time of the interview, she says the threatened presidential litigation task force had not yet acted. Separately, she reports xAI litigation against California and Colorado transparency rules and attributes Colorado’s substantial weakening of its laws partly to such threats. Her expectation that the campaign will impede legislation is a prediction.
qs: I think the claim to state capacity to regulate AI is strong
Unfortunately, I also believe there’s a successful political campaign against these laws, and that’s going to stymie the development of legislation in this area.
We haven’t seen that happen yet, but many states recognize that the threat is real.

So xAI has been suing in California and Colorado to undermine AI transparency rules, and they’ve been pretty successful. Colorado revisited and substantially weakened its laws partly in response to these threats.

kp.k: National-security arguments do not establish deregulation’s necessity
kp.d: Bloch-Wehba reports, rather than endorses, the argument that an AI arms race requires avoiding restrictions on development. She challenges its premise by stating that China regulates AI and uses nuclear weapons as an analogy against assuming that national security requires a wholly deregulatory environment.
qs: The problem is that, first, China does regulate AI, so the whole idea that they have hands-off development and we need it too doesn’t work.
Second, it’s this assumption that you need a totally deregulatory environment to safeguard national security, but we would never have said that about nuclear weapons, for example.

kp.k: Public journalism funding could reduce platform dependence
kp.d: As a cross-domain institutional proposal, Bloch-Wehba argues that requiring platforms to compensate news organizations does not resolve editorial independence concerns. She proposes a public but meaningfully independent journalism foundation, drawing on NSF peer review while acknowledging that this model is contested and not straightforward to transplant. She prioritizes civic-value journalism in geographically underserved communities. A possible AI-tax revenue stream is speculative and intended to reduce political leverage associated with congressional appropriations; the funding design remains unresolved.
qs: I think you’re no more independent
if you take your money from Google than if you take your money from the government.
The National Science Foundation dealt with that through institutions of independent peer review, essentially.
My first order of business would be geographically underserved communities.

I could see a revenue source that comes from some kind of AI tax and removes at least some of the levers political actors have to bully these agencies or force them to adopt a political agenda that would compromise the integrity and independence of journalistic institutions.

kp.k: Grassroots opposition increases technology accountability’s public visibility
kp.d: Looking back over the preceding year, Bloch-Wehba identifies opposition to data centers and Flock surveillance cameras as emerging or intensifying sources of public mobilization. She interprets this as increased visibility of technology’s entanglement with government and a rapidly changing political conversation in an election year. These are qualitative observations, not measured public-opinion findings.
qs: Opposition to data centers is becoming a high-profile grassroots issue that I didn’t expect or see a year ago today, although I think the ball was rolling.
issues related to tech accountability and tech’s enmeshment in the state are much more visible to people than they were a year ago.
That means the political conversation about these things is changing quite quickly, especially because it’s an election year.

kp.k: Higher education faces uncertain AI-related transformation
kp.d: Asked for a forecast, Bloch-Wehba anticipates significant changes to universities, research and law schools over the next few years, partly because of AI, workforce changes and internal institutional shifts. She repeatedly emphasizes uncertainty about their form. The stronger suggestion that her children might not attend college within the next 20 years is her husband’s view, which she does not endorse. She places these concerns within a broader claimed deterioration and transformation of journalism, publishing, search and learning.
qs: there are significant changes coming to higher education. I don’t know what they are.
That’s partly because of technological change in AI. I think there are going to be questions about the role of higher education as the workforce changes, which I think is going to happen fast.
For people who have kids in college, going to college in the future, or going to graduate school or law school, these are going to be different places than they are right now.
So the whole information ecosystem, how people learn, is changing quickly.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Sam Moore reports that legal-sector AI governance is shifting from prohibitions toward risk differentiation and client-facing explanations.
pts.d: In the opening advisory segment, Moore says most law firms and law departments have some AI policy. He describes a current movement away from restrictive first-generation policies toward distinguishing routine, low-risk uses from more substantial uses. He identifies making policies understandable enough for every legal-team member to explain to clients as an unresolved industry challenge. These are practitioner observations and expectations, not measured adoption findings.

pts.k: Hannah Bloch-Wehba argues that public dependence on private technology infrastructure complicates constitutional accountability and creates durable vendor lock-in.
pts.d: This is a broader technology-governance claim, not specifically a claim about generative AI or law-firm productivity. Bloch-Wehba attributes technology companies’ central position partly to affirmative federal support for science and innovation over decades, rather than deregulation alone. She argues that companies supplying government’s informational infrastructure are difficult to classify under traditional state-action doctrine. Long-duration infrastructure relationships can persist despite political turnover because switching costs and anti-competitive effects constrain elected officials. Her Department of the Interior–Google contract example is explicitly hypothetical.

pts.k: Bloch-Wehba argues that trade-secret protection for investigative technologies impedes defendants’ challenges and the public production of evidence about whether tools work.
pts.d: Discussing privately developed data and algorithmic tools in criminal enforcement, she says vendor secrecy can prevent defendants from accessing information needed to challenge evidence used in arrests or convictions. She also identifies a systemic consequence: where tools have not been meaningfully tested before deployment, obstructing adversarial examination prevents the litigation process from exposing their validity. This concerns investigative technology generally; she does not identify a generative-model error rate or a named criminal case.

pts.k: Bloch-Wehba presents Google’s geofence practices as an example of corporate data governance determining police capabilities and practical legal requirements.
pts.d: In this non-AI-specific example, she argues that Google’s location collection and storage made geofence investigations possible, while its corporate policy required police to obtain warrants. She says Google’s 2023 decision to stop default Sensorvault location storage subsequently curtailed that investigative possibility. She distinguishes substantive outcomes from institutional accountability: she considers the warrant requirement appropriate and the later change beneficial for privacy, but objects to a company determining these matters according to its own preferences and burdens.

pts.k: Bloch-Wehba argues that AI accountability requires complementary information mechanisms and predicts that political and litigation pressure will inhibit state legislation.
pts.d: Drawing on her review of proposed and enacted state AI legislation, she characterizes these measures as requirements to generate and share product information with different audiences. She rejects a single best accountability instrument, advocating public information, researcher access and direct regulatory disclosure together. She believes state capacity to regulate remains strong, but says preemption threats, threatened funding cuts and litigation deter experimentation. She cites xAI litigation in California and Colorado and Colorado’s subsequent weakening of its law as examples. She challenges the argument that national security requires a wholly deregulatory environment, noting that China regulates AI and drawing an analogy with nuclear-weapons regulation.

pts.k: Bloch-Wehba argues that platform-funded journalism does not resolve independence concerns and proposes AI-tax-supported public funding as a possible alternative.
pts.d: Within journalism, she argues that receiving money from influential technology platforms can compromise independence just as government funding can. She proposes a public but meaningfully independent journalism institution, using independent peer review as an institutional reference point. She suggests that an AI-derived revenue source could reduce some political leverage associated with appropriations. This is a conditional institutional proposal, not evidence of an implemented funding model or a prediction that an AI tax will be enacted. She prioritizes civic-value journalism in geographically underserved communities.

pts.k: Bloch-Wehba observes growing grassroots opposition to data centers and surveillance cameras, making technology accountability more politically visible.
pts.d: She describes opposition to data centers and Flock surveillance cameras as an emerging popular movement. She interprets this as increased visibility of technology companies’ relationships with the state and a rapidly changing political conversation. The claim concerns infrastructure and surveillance governance, rather than legal-market substitution; the transcript does not quantify participation or establish that all the relevant infrastructure is AI-specific.

pts.k: Bloch-Wehba anticipates substantial changes to higher education, including law schools, partly because AI will change the workforce.
pts.d: She expects core assumptions about higher education’s functions to change and anticipates rapid workforce change, but explicitly declines to specify the future institutional form. She also attributes change to developments within universities rather than AI alone. Her prediction encompasses undergraduate, graduate and legal education. The stronger suggestion that her children may not attend college in 20 years is attributed to her husband and is not adopted as her own prediction.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on advisory experience, scholarly research, institutional examples and qualitative observation rather than quantitative AI-performance or legal-labor evidence.
pts.d: Moore grounds his governance observations in Legal Technology Hub’s client conversations and policy-revision work, presented alongside an invitation to use its advisory services. Bloch-Wehba draws on her historical research for “How Tech Took Over,” a review of state AI legislation for “Information Law Pluralism,” her work on criminal investigative technologies, and the Google geofence example. For regulation, she cites litigation and Colorado’s legislative response without case citations or effect measurements. Her journalism proposal draws on four years of press-freedom litigation experience and analogies to the NSF and public broadcasting. Her higher-education prediction and observations about mobilization are qualitative judgments. The transcript supplies no model benchmarks, survey sample, employment estimates or measured causal effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims span current governance changes, decades-long infrastructure dependence, near-term regulatory constraints and explicitly uncertain educational forecasts.
pts.d: In the document’s 2026 context, Moore contrasts present policy development with policies written in 2023–2024. Bloch-Wehba traces government support for technology back to the 1930s–1940s and describes lock-in as a decades-long issue, not a single-administration problem. Trade-secrecy obstacles have been emerging for several years and arise when vendor secrecy blocks scrutiny of evidentiary tools. Google’s storage-policy change is dated to 2023. Her state-legislation review began a couple of years before the interview; she distinguishes existing litigation from a threatened presidential litigation task force that she says had not yet materialized. Public mobilization is compared with one year earlier. Higher-education change is anticipated over the next few years without a precise endpoint; AI-tax funding remains conditional.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include legal teams and clients, criminal defendants, public institutions, AI providers, news organizations and students.
pts.d: Law firms and in-house legal departments face governance and client-communication demands. Criminal defendants and defense counsel face limits on challenging technological evidence; the public loses opportunities to learn whether investigative tools work. Police capabilities and requirements depend on private data practices, while individuals’ location privacy is affected. Government agencies and elected officials face switching costs and accountability problems. AI providers face disclosure obligations, while researchers, regulators, affected individuals and the public need different kinds of information. News organizations risk dependence on influential funders, with underserved communities prioritized in the proposed alternative. Communities around infrastructure and surveillance systems are described as mobilizing politically. Universities, researchers, families, and future law and graduate students face uncertain institutional change. The source makes no concrete forecast of lawyer job losses, law-firm staffing ratios, billing changes or AI-driven legal-market shares.
